notes: Second appeal on late witness statement and medical confidentiality; Brooke LJ grants conditional permission on condition.

enrichment.short_title: Roberts v Williams: late witness statement and confidential medical evidence
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Roberts retained a right of way over Beechways after selling it to Mr and Mrs Williams, who later placed boulders and built a wall obstructing access.
District Judge Godwin refused permission to adduce a late witness statement from Mrs Williams dated 27 March 2004, shortly before trial in May 2004.
Mrs Williams' statement alleged solicitor Mr Phillips had twice approved their planned works; illness was asserted at the hearing but no medical evidence was before the district judge.
Judge Denyer QC upheld the refusal after Mrs Williams sought to show a confidential medical report only to the judge and claimants' lawyers, not the claimants themselves.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal application for permission to appeal interlocutory refusal to admit late witness evidence in a county court right-of-way dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on condition the defendants pay about £1,400 in prior costs orders within 14 days; otherwise permission lapses; matter listed for a three-judge court.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant is so sensitive about medical evidence that neighbours cannot see it, a judge may properly refuse to determine admissibility on that basis alone; whether late evidence should nonetheless be admitted on appropriate cost sanctions is an important practice point warranting full appellate consideration.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Denyer was entitled to refuse to examine confidential medical evidence
Whether Mrs Williams' late statement should have been admitted given asserted illness and proximity to trial
Whether the district judge acted within discretion in refusing the evidence
Appropriate conditions for granting permission on a second appeal

confidence.notes: Interlocutory permission decision with clear reasoning though final trial merits remain undetermined.

notes: Landmark commissioned copyright appeal; Court of Appeal endorses Lightman J principles and dismisses appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Griggs v Evans: implied assignment of copyright in combined Doc Martens logo
key_facts: Freelance designer Ross Evans created a combined Dr Martens and airWair logo for Griggs via advertising agency Irwin Jordan at £15 per hour for UK point-of-sale material.
Evans was first legal owner of worldwide copyright and later assigned legal title to Australian defendant Dr Martens Pty in May 2002.
Griggs contended the agency contract implied full beneficial ownership of the logo, not merely a limited UK POS licence.
The deputy judge held a logo commission ordinarily requires implied assignment so the client can exclude competitors and enforce copyright globally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Deputy High Court declaration that Griggs were equitable owners of copyright in the combined logo; appeal on foreign-rights point abandoned.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Griggs established as beneficial owners entitled to legal assignment of worldwide copyrights.
enrichment.ratio: Where a freelance designer is commissioned to create a corporate logo, business efficacy ordinarily implies the client receives full copyright rather than a minimal licence; references to 'UK point of sale' in order documents identify the work, not the scope of rights granted.
legal_issues: Whether copyright in a commissioned logo vested in the client or the freelance author
Application of Lightman J's principles in Robin Ray v Classic FM
Whether invoice wording limited rights to UK point-of-sale use
Whether foreign copyright could be assigned by English court orders
linked_authorities: Robin Ray v Classic FM [1998] FSR 622
Liverpool City Council v Irwin [1977] AC 239
BP Refinery (Westernport) Pty Ltd v Hastings (1978) 52 ALJR 20

confidence.notes: Detailed endorsement of established commissioning principles with clear final disposition.

notes: Lord Slynn's final domestic sitting; magistrates' jurisdiction on CSA liability orders restored.

enrichment.short_title: Farley v SoS: magistrates' jurisdiction to question child support liability
key_facts: Mr Farley challenged a liability order for £32,639.94 arrears, arguing the Secretary of State lacked jurisdiction because a written maintenance agreement existed and section 6 benefit conditions were unproved.
North Somerset justices held section 33(4) prevented them questioning the maintenance assessment's validity and made the liability order.
Keith J dismissed the case stated appeal, treating 'liable person' as a person the Secretary of State had assessed rather than a person legally liable under the Act.
Farley sought to rely on a July 1999 maintenance agreement and absence of proved authorising benefit receipt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' liability order under section 33 Child Support Act 1991.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; liability order set aside; case remitted; magistrates held to have adjudicative function on whether the non-resident parent was a liable person and to require evidence of benefit claims where disputed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 33(4) precludes questioning the calculation of maintenance, not whether the Secretary of State had jurisdiction to make an assessment; magistrates must be satisfied payments became payable by a person actually liable, especially where enforcement may lead to committal and no adequate alternative challenge existed.
legal_issues: Whether section 33(4) bars inquiry into initial liability or only quantum
Meaning of 'liable person' in section 33(1) and (3)
Whether magistrates must receive evidence of section 6 benefit authorisation
Availability of review or appeal against section 6 decisions
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for Social Security v Shotton [1996] 2 FLR 241
Secretary of State for Social Security v Harmon [1998] 2 FLR 598

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and remittal order clearly reasoned across three appellate judgments.

notes: Attorney General's unduly lenient sentence reference; concurrent sentences for distinct serious offences criticised.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 138 of 2004: unduly lenient sentence for Shane White
key_facts: Shane White pleaded guilty to drug supply and possession offences, conspiracy to commit gross indecency with a child, and false imprisonment of Jason Cutter.
Police ran a fortified Hereford flat as a senior drug supplier; CCTV captured humiliation of Cutter and grooming of a 10-year-old boy.
Crown Court imposed concurrent sentences totalling five years, including 15 months for the child offence and 18 months for false imprisonment.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient, particularly because distinct serious non-drug offences were ordered concurrent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 for unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; total sentence increased to eight years comprising five years on drugs (unchanged), concurrent two-and-a-half years for false imprisonment, and three years consecutive for the child offence.
enrichment.ratio: False imprisonment used to enforce a drug empire and deliberate gross indecency involving a child are separate grave offences that should attract substantial consecutive sentences; concurrent treatment with drug counts was unjustified even allowing credit for guilty pleas and totality.
legal_issues: Whether the overall five-year sentence was unduly lenient
Appropriate consecutive or concurrent structure for drug, false imprisonment and child indecency counts
Minimum sentences for false imprisonment and conspiracy to commit gross indecency
Application of R v Dhajit to Class A drug supply at dealer level
linked_authorities: R v Dhajit [1999] 2 Cr App R(S) 142

confidence.notes: Facts, individual counts and revised sentence structure are explicitly set out.

notes: Lord Chancellor refuses permission on paper under existing civil restraint order; vexatious applications.

enrichment.short_title: Perotti v Bird & Bird: refusal of permission to appeal strike-out and restraint
key_facts: Mr Perotti sought permission to appeal Evans-Lombe J's orders striking out a solicitors' negligence claim and making a general civil restraint order.
An earlier specific civil restraint order required paper-only consideration with final determination on the papers.
The Lord Chancellor found the applications totally devoid of merit and the 56-page supplemental material largely irrelevant and unintelligible.
Evans-Lombe J struck out the claim as an abuse of process under Johnson v Gore Wood and Bairstow principles and as statute-barred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written application for permission to appeal strike-out and general civil restraint orders under an existing civil restraint regime.
enrichment.outcome: All applications for permission to appeal and related applications refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant subject to civil restraint submits sprawling, abusive material without addressing why strike-out or a general restraint order was wrong, permission to appeal should be refused; a transcript may exceptionally be ordered where the judge referred to it, but that does not imply merit.
legal_issues: Whether the negligence claim was an abuse of process
Whether the claim was statute-barred
Lawfulness of a general civil restraint order
Effect of existing specific civil restraint requiring paper disposal
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood [2002] 2 AC 1
Secretary of State for Trade and Industry v Bairstow [2004] EWCA Civ 880

confidence.notes: Short procedural disposal with clear grounds though underlying claim details are not fully rehearsed.

notes: Lord Chief Justice guidance on guilty plea discounts for mandatory life murder minimum terms under CJA 2003.

enrichment.short_title: Last v R: guilty plea reductions for murder minimum terms
key_facts: Five conjoined appeals concerned minimum terms for murder after guilty pleas under the Criminal Justice Act 2003 regime.
Emma Last's minimum term was reduced from about 20 to 17 years equivalent after full one-sixth guilty plea discount proved excessive relative to co-defendant Bauer.
Sarah Crane's late plea appeal was dismissed; Holbrook's minimum term was increased from 12 to 20 years on Solicitor General reference.
Quillan brothers' appeals were dismissed where a 30-year Schedule 21 starting point was justified for robbery murder of an elderly victim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined Court of Appeal judgments on minimum term appeals and an unduly lenient sentence reference for murder after guilty pleas.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance issued on guilty plea reductions for murder; Last appeal allowed in part; Crane and Quillan appeals dismissed; Holbrook minimum term increased to 20 years.
enrichment.ratio: For murder minimum terms the guilty plea reduction is capped at one-sixth or five years whichever is less, with a sliding scale down to about 5% for late pleas; because the minimum term equals time in custody before parole, discounts have greater effect than on determinate sentences and must be applied after calculating seriousness under Schedule 21.
legal_issues: Appropriate discount for guilty pleas in mandatory life murder sentences
Whether Sentencing Guidelines Council guilty plea guidance applies retrospectively
Interaction of Schedule 21 starting points and Schedule 22 transitional provisions
Disparity between co-defendants' minimum terms after guilty pleas
linked_authorities: R v Sullivan & Others [2004] EWCA Crim 1762
Anderson v DPP [2003] 1 AC 837

notes: Permission granted on Sinclair fraud tracing issues; personal fiduciary duty and fraud-based constructive trust points.

enrichment.short_title: Sinclair v Versailles: permission on fraud tracing and director fiduciary duty
key_facts: Sinclair advanced £2.35 million to Versailles Trade Finance Ltd's factoring business, but funds were misused in cross-firing fraud by directors Cushnie and Clough.
Marrlist Ltd profits from selling Versailles shares funded a Kensington property whose £8.6 million sale proceeds were paid to administrative receivers.
Sinclair pleaded constructive trust claims based on personal fiduciary duties owed by Cushnie and on fraud-based constructive trust over profits.
Deputy judge allowed Kensington claim to proceed to trial; Peter Gibson LJ granted permission on two points of principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal refusal of strike-out on the Kensington constructive trust claim in Versailles fraud litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on whether a company director can owe a personal fiduciary duty to an investor and on whether fraud profits must be held on constructive trust; tracing amendment appeal also permitted.
enrichment.ratio: Important points of principle arise where a director allegedly assumes personal fiduciary responsibilities to an investor and where fraudulent misuse of funds enables subsequent profits; such issues may warrant full appeal even if fact-finding at trial is ultimately required.
legal_issues: Whether a director can owe fiduciary duties directly to an external investor
Whether profits from share sales funded by fraud must be held on constructive trust for the defrauded investor
Scope of Westdeutsche Landesbank fraud-based constructive trust principles
Whether equitable tracing into Kensington sale proceeds is arguable
linked_authorities: Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale v Islington London Borough Council [1996] AC 676
Halifax Building Society v Thomas [1996] Ch 217
Foskett v McKeown [2001] 1 AC 102

notes: Short supplemental costs and case management order in Dumford shipping guarantee litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Dumford v Atlantrybflot: reserved costs and case management directions
key_facts: This is a supplemental Court of Appeal hearing following the main Dumford guarantee appeal judgment.
Costs below and of the appeal, including costs before Lord Justice Clarke, were reserved for the Commercial Court judge.
Leave to appeal to the House of Lords and a_striker order were refused.
Security for costs remains in court pending a Part 24 application; jurisdiction challenge to be heard before the Commercial Court judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental Court of Appeal directions on costs and case management after judgment in guarantee summary judgment appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Costs reserved; House of Lords leave and_striker order refused; security for costs retained; actions to be listed together; jurisdiction challenge and Part 24 application sequencing left to Commercial Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where overall liability remains to be finally determined, appellate costs may properly be reserved for the trial judge to apply Gough or section 51 principles according to the ultimate outcome; procedural sequencing should allow jurisdiction challenges before summary judgment applications where logical.
legal_issues: Whether Gough v Gough or section 51 costs rules should apply
Timing of jurisdiction challenge relative to Part 24 application
Treatment of security for costs pending further interlocutory applications
Listing of related actions together

notes: Post-trial costs order after failed magazine copyright claim; indemnity costs and interest on costs awarded.

enrichment.short_title: IPC Media v Highbury: indemnity costs after failed IDEAL HOME copyright claim
key_facts: IPC Media sued Highbury Leisure alleging HOME magazine covers and articles copied artistic copyright in IDEAL HOME.
After a three-week trial Laddie J held the claim wholly without merit with no copying found.
Highbury sought interest on costs at 1% above base from invoice dates and indemnity costs from three months after a Part 36 offer.
Combined litigation costs exceeded £1.8 million due to the claimant's wide, shifting allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for post-judgment costs order including interest on costs and indemnity basis assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Action dismissed with costs; £350,000 interim payment agreed; interest on costs ordered from invoice dates at 1% above base; indemnity costs ordered from 9 July 2003.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 44.3 permits interest on pre-judgment costs to reflect the real cost of funding litigation; indemnity costs are compensatory not penal and may be ordered where a thin, high-risk copyright claim pursued unreasonably takes a case out of the norm despite bona fide belief.
legal_issues: Whether interest should run on costs before judgment under CPR 44.3(6)(g)
Whether indemnity costs were warranted without moral turpitude
Effect of Part 36 offer and detailed independent-design defence
Appropriate costs consequences of an unusually expensive artistic copyright claim
linked_authorities: Bim Kemi AB v Blackburn Chemicals Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 889
Excelsior Commercial and Industrial Holdings Ltd v Salisbury [2002] EWCA Civ 879
Hunt v R M Douglas (Roofing) Ltd [1990] 1 AC 398

notes: Commercial Court Part 24 guarantee appeal allowed; misnomer, assignment and corporate identity issues.

enrichment.short_title: Dumford v Atlantrybflot: Part 24 set aside on guarantee party identity
key_facts: Dumford lent $2.1 million to Shelley Marketing LLC guaranteed by documents naming ZAO Atalantribflot, but summary judgment was entered against OAO Atlantrybflot.
Guarantees referred to ZAO's registered office at 19 Karl Marx Street Kaliningrad, which was OAO's postal address; ZAO's registered office was in Moscow.
Dumford assigned loan rights to Mauritanian Mauribalt SA to arrest a vessel, raising title-to-sue issues under clause 16.3.
The judge used extrinsic evidence to treat OAO as guarantor; the Court of Appeal held real issues existed on misnomer, construction and assignment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Part 24 summary judgment for about £1.89 million on loan guarantees; jurisdiction and assignment defences raised.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment quashed; matter remitted to Commercial Court; costs reserved; security for costs retained pending further Part 24 application.
enrichment.ratio: Where two distinct Russian corporate entities exist and guarantees consistently name ZAO while extrinsic evidence suggests OAO, summary judgment is unsafe on misnomer or construction grounds; a prohibited or disputed assignment to a non-financial institution also raises a real issue as to the claimant's title to sue.
legal_issues: Whether references to ZAO were mere misnomer for OAO
Use of extrinsic evidence to construe guarantor identity
Whether Dumford retained title to sue after assignment to Mauribalt SA
Effect of clause 16.3 restricting assignment to banks or financial institutions
linked_authorities: Davies v Elsby Brothers Ltd [1961] 1 WLR 170
Shogun Finance Ltd v Hudson [2003] UKHL 62
Linden Gardens Trust Ltd v Lenesta Sludge Disposals Ltd [1994] 1 AC 85
Amalgamated Investment & Property Co Ltd v Texas Commerce International Bank Ltd [1982] 1 QB 84
